subtype: Approach: greed-driven engagement with a prize offer [Pitfall]
passage: Counsellor's note, Thursday. Swati (Class 9) came to my room looking pale. She told me a message had promised a free phone if she paid a small delivery fee. She had imagined the phone in her hand all evening. She paid two hundred rupees using a wallet, and then a second message asked for more. When she ignored it, the messages stopped and the phone never came. “I feel so stupid,” she said. I told her scammers depend on excitement, not on people being foolish, and that it was not her fault. We rang her parents that afternoon, and they reported it to the bank. Swati asked me to help her write a short rule: free things never need payment first. — Jasleen

qa.q: How did Swati pay the fee?
What was Swati feeling after the messages stopped?
qa.a: Embarrassed and upset: she said she felt stupid and blamed herself.

qa.q: What could Swati do next time, and why?
qa.a: Treat any prize that asks for money first as a warning, and check with an adult before paying, since real prizes do not need a payment up front.

qa.q: How does the situation look to the counsellor?
qa.a: Jasleen sees a student tricked through excitement instead of foolishness, and wants her to feel supported and not blamed.

grounding: A teen imagines winning a free phone and pays a small fee, discovering that free prizes needing payment are a standard trick.

passage:
Thursday
Writing this so I remember how today felt. At lunch a message came: “Congratulations! You've won a new phone in our lucky draw. Pay a small delivery charge to claim.” I don't even remember entering any draw. But I kept picturing it: a new phone, showing Anjali, finally no cracked screen.
The charge was small, so I paid it from the wallet app before I could think. The page said “processing”. Then nothing. The number stopped replying.
After school Anjali showed me a clip on her phone about exactly this: prize, small fee, gone. Free things that make you pay first aren't free. I felt sick.
I told Mumma at dinner. She wasn't angry, just quiet. Then she reported the number with me through the wallet app's help section and blocked it.
– Alka

qa.q: What did the message ask Alka to pay?
qa.a: A small delivery charge to claim the phone.

qa.q: What was Alka feeling after Anjali showed the clip?
qa.a: Alka felt sick and foolish, realising the prize was a trick and the money was gone.

qa.q: What would have helped Alka pause before paying?
qa.a: Asking whether any draw had been entered, and showing the message to Mumma or Anjali first, since a real prize doesn't ask for payment.

qa.q: How might Mumma feel hearing about it at dinner?
qa.a: Mumma may feel worried and a little sad, but also glad Alka told her the same day so they could report and block the number.

grounding: Shows a teen paying a small fee for a free phone prize, getting nothing, and later seeing that prizes that demand payment are a known trick.
